title: Vraylar and Alcohol: Risks, Timing, and What Your Label Says
excerpt: Can you drink on Vraylar? How cariprazine and alcohol interact, why its weeks-long half-life makes dose timing pointless, the risks for mood, and the signs that need care.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Vraylar? How cariprazine and alcohol interact, why dose timing doesn't help, side effects to watch for, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the safest choice is to avoid alcohol while you take Vraylar (cariprazine). There's no dramatic chemical reaction between the two in your blood. The problem is that both act on the brain, and together they can make you sleepier, dizzier, and less steady than either one alone. Alcohol also tends to work against the very things Vraylar is prescribed for, especially in bipolar disorder and depression. And because cariprazine stays in your body for weeks, there's no time of day when it's "worn off" and a drink is clear of it.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink until you know how Vraylar affects you, which realistically means a few weeks on a steady dose, since its effects build slowly. Never skip or stop a dose so you can drink; it won't clear your system in time and missing doses can bring symptoms back. If you and your prescriber decide an occasional drink is acceptable, stick to the amount they set, have it with food and water, and don't drive afterward. If you drink most weeks, tell your prescriber honestly. They can only plan around what they know.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who knows your diagnosis, dose, and other medicines. **Talk to your prescriber before drinking on Vraylar,** especially if you take it for bipolar disorder, take other sedating medicines, are over 65, or have a history of seizures, fainting, or heavy drinking. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** someone on Vraylar who has been drinking can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, faints, has a seizure, vomits while barely conscious, or develops a high fever with stiff muscles and confusion. **If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide or self-harm, call or text 988** (the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline), or call 911. If you're outside the US, contact your local emergency number.

## What Vraylar Is and Why People Take It

Vraylar is the brand name for **cariprazine**, a prescription medicine in the group called atypical (or second-generation) antipsychotics. It comes as a once-daily capsule. Like several drugs in this class, it's prescribed for more than psychosis. In the US it's approved for:

- **Schizophrenia** in adults
- **Bipolar I disorder**, to treat manic or mixed episodes
- **Bipolar depression**, the depressive episodes of bipolar I disorder
- **Major depressive disorder**, as an add-on to an antidepressant when the antidepressant alone hasn't done enough

Because of those last two uses, a lot of people taking Vraylar aren't thinking of themselves as "on an antipsychotic" at all. They're taking a small dose alongside an antidepressant, or for bipolar depression. That's exactly the group most likely to wonder whether a glass of wine at dinner is fine, so it's worth understanding what the medicine actually does.

### How it works, briefly

Cariprazine is a **partial agonist** at dopamine D2 and D3 receptors. "Partial agonist" means it partly switches those receptors on rather than fully blocking them, so it can turn dopamine signalling down where it's too high and nudge it up where it's too low. What makes cariprazine stand out is how strongly it binds the **D3 receptor**, more strongly than most other antipsychotics. D3 receptors are involved in mood, motivation, and reward. Cariprazine also acts on serotonin receptors (it's a partial agonist at 5-HT1A and blocks 5-HT2A), which is part of why it helps with depression.

In practice, Vraylar tends to be **less sedating than drugs like quetiapine (Seroquel) or olanzapine**. Many people find it more activating than sleepy. But "less sedating" doesn't mean "not sedating." Sleepiness and dizziness appear among its reported side effects, and its most common side effect, an inner restlessness called **akathisia**, interacts with drinking in its own way, covered below.

## How Vraylar and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Pharmacists split drug interactions into two kinds. A **pharmacokinetic** interaction is when one substance changes how much of the other ends up in your blood, usually by speeding up or slowing down the liver enzymes that clear it. A **pharmacodynamic** interaction is when two substances act on the same systems in your body and their effects add up.

Cariprazine is broken down mainly by a liver enzyme called **CYP3A4**, with a smaller role for one called CYP2D6. Alcohol isn't known to significantly change cariprazine levels in the way that some antifungals or seizure medicines do, and there's no formal study showing alcohol raises or lowers them. So the Vraylar and alcohol problem is mainly **pharmacodynamic**. Here's what that looks like.

### 1. Stacked drowsiness and slowed reactions

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. It slows your reaction time, coordination, and judgment. Vraylar, like other antipsychotics, carries a label warning that it may impair judgment, thinking, and motor skills, and patients are told not to drive or use dangerous machinery until they know how it affects them. When the two overlap, the impairment can be more than you'd predict from the number of drinks. People often describe one drink hitting like two.

### 2. Dizziness and fainting when you stand up

Antipsychotics as a group can cause **orthostatic hypotension**, a drop in blood pressure when you go from lying or sitting to standing. The Vraylar prescribing information lists it, along with fainting, as a warning. Alcohol widens blood vessels and makes you lose fluid, which pushes blood pressure in the same direction. The combination can leave you light-headed, with blurry vision, or fainting when you get off the couch or out of bed at night. The label also lists **falls** as a risk, and alcohol makes falls more likely on its own.

### 3. Restlessness (akathisia) and the urge to "take the edge off"

Akathisia is a feeling of inner restlessness, an urge to keep moving, pace, or shift in your seat. In Vraylar's clinical trials it was one of the most commonly reported side effects, and it's more likely at higher doses. Some people notice that a drink in the evening seems to calm it down. That's worth telling your prescriber about rather than managing on your own, for two reasons. First, there are real medical fixes for akathisia, including dose changes and other medicines. Second, alcohol fragments sleep in the second half of the night, and poor sleep tends to leave you more restless and on edge the next day, so the relief doesn't last.

### 4. Body temperature and dehydration

The label warns that antipsychotics can disrupt the body's ability to lower its core temperature, and advises avoiding overheating and dehydration. Alcohol makes you lose fluid and can dull your sense of being too hot. A long afternoon drinking outdoors in summer, a hot festival, or a crowded dance floor are the situations where this matters most.

### 5. Seizure threshold

The Vraylar label includes a warning to use it with caution in people with a history of seizures, a warning shared across the antipsychotic class. Heavy drinking, and especially the withdrawal period after a run of heavy drinking, can also make seizures more likely. For most social drinkers this isn't a day-to-day concern, but it's one more reason a prescriber needs to know about a history of heavy drinking or seizures.

## What the Label and Official Guidance Actually Say

The Vraylar prescribing information and patient Medication Guide don't give a "safe" number of drinks. What they do include are warnings that alcohol can make worse:

- Don't drive or operate machinery until you know how Vraylar affects you.
- Sleepiness and impaired judgment, thinking, and motor skills.
- Orthostatic hypotension, fainting, and falls.
- Trouble regulating body temperature; avoid overheating and dehydration.
- Seizures, and difficulty swallowing.
- Metabolic changes: weight gain, higher blood sugar, and changes in cholesterol and triglycerides. Alcohol adds calories and can affect blood sugar and triglycerides too.

Vraylar also carries **two boxed warnings**, the strongest kind the FDA uses. One is about an increased risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis, which is shared by all antipsychotics. The other is about **suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, teens, and young adults**, which applies because of its use in depression. Alcohol is linked with low mood and impulsive acts, which is part of why drinking is a particular concern for younger people taking Vraylar.

General drug references and pharmacists usually advise avoiding or limiting alcohol with any antipsychotic for these reasons. If you've been told something different by your own prescriber, who knows your history and dose, their advice takes priority over any general article, including this one.

## Can You Drink on Vraylar at All? The "Just One Drink" Question

This is what most people really want to know, so here's an honest way to think about it.

**The safest answer is no.** Avoiding alcohol removes the extra drowsiness, dizziness, and fall risk, and it removes alcohol's effect on mood and sleep.

**The real-world answer depends on you.** Many prescribers are more worried about regular or heavy drinking than about a single drink at a celebration for someone who has been stable for months on a low dose. Whether that applies to you depends on:

- **Your dose.** Someone on 1.5 mg as an add-on for depression is in a different position from someone on 6 mg for schizophrenia.
- **How long you've been on it.** Cariprazine's effects build over several weeks (more on that below). Side effects like restlessness can also show up later than you'd expect. The first month or two, and the weeks after any dose change, are the worst time to experiment.
- **What it's treating.** For bipolar disorder, alcohol is a well-known trigger for mood episodes. Your prescriber may want you to avoid it entirely for that reason alone.
- **Your other medicines.** Vraylar is often taken with an antidepressant, a mood stabilizer like lithium or lamotrigine, a sleep aid, or an anti-anxiety medicine. Every extra sedating drug raises the stakes.
- **Your history with alcohol.** If drinking has caused problems before, that changes the conversation completely.

If you've talked it through with your prescriber and they're comfortable with an occasional drink, these habits keep the risk lower:

1. Stick to **the amount your prescriber agreed**, drink it slowly, and have it with a meal.
2. Drink water alongside it.
3. **Don't drive** or do anything that needs quick reactions afterward. Sort out your ride home before you go.
4. Stand up slowly, and be careful on stairs and in the bathroom at night.
5. Don't stack other sedating things that evening, such as sleep aids, sedating antihistamines, cannabis, or opioid painkillers.
6. Pay attention to how you feel. If one drink hits much harder than it used to, that's useful information to pass on.

## Cariprazine and Alcohol: Is the Generic Name Any Different?

No. Cariprazine is the active ingredient in Vraylar, so "cariprazine and alcohol" and "Vraylar and alcohol" are the same question. Everything in this article applies to any cariprazine product, whatever it's called where you live.

## Timing: How Long After Vraylar Can You Drink?

A common plan is to take your capsule in the morning and have a drink in the evening, hoping the two won't overlap. With cariprazine, that idea doesn't hold up, and the reason is unusual even among antipsychotics.

- **Cariprazine itself has a long half-life,** roughly 2 to 4 days according to the label. A half-life is the time it takes for the amount in your body to fall by half.
- **Its active breakdown products last much longer.** The body turns cariprazine into two active metabolites. The main one, didesmethyl-cariprazine (DDCAR), has a half-life of about 1 to 3 weeks, and it makes up most of the active drug in your blood once you're on regular dosing.
- **It takes weeks to reach a steady level.** The label notes that the total active drug takes about 3 weeks to reach steady state, and that it can take several weeks for levels to fall after you stop. Because of this, the label also warns that side effects may appear several weeks after starting the medicine or changing the dose.

So once you're on regular dosing, the amount of active drug in your system is nearly the same at 9 pm as it was at 9 am. Spacing your capsule and your drink by a few hours, or even a day, doesn't separate them in any meaningful way.

What timing *can* help with is the alcohol side. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies a lot between people. Waiting until the alcohol has fully cleared before driving, or before taking another sedating medicine that night, is still sensible.

## Don't Skip or Stop Vraylar So You Can Drink

Some people think about skipping a dose before a night out, a wedding, or a holiday. It's a bad trade.

**It doesn't work.** With active drug lasting weeks in the body, skipping one capsule (or even several) barely changes the level in your blood. You'd still be drinking with Vraylar on board.

**It can backfire.** Missing doses can raise the chance that the symptoms you're treating return, whether that's a manic or depressive episode, a slide back into depression, or a return of psychosis. Because cariprazine leaves the body so slowly, a relapse after stopping can also creep up over weeks, which makes it easy to miss the connection. If you want more flexibility around alcohol, or you're unhappy with the medicine, talk with your prescriber about changing the plan rather than adjusting it yourself.

## Alcohol, Mood, and the Conditions Vraylar Treats

Even apart from the drug interaction, alcohol tends to pull in the opposite direction from Vraylar.

**Bipolar disorder.** Alcohol use is common in people with bipolar disorder, and research has consistently linked it with more frequent mood episodes, poorer sleep, and a weaker response to treatment. Sleep loss is a well-known trigger for mania, and alcohol disrupts sleep. The lift from a few drinks can also blur the line between a fun night and the start of a high. If you take Vraylar alongside lithium, our [lithium and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/lithium-and-alcohol) covers the extra issues with dehydration and lithium levels.

**Bipolar depression and major depression.** Alcohol is a depressant. It can lift mood for an hour and then pull it down for a day or two after. Many people find their worst low days follow drinking. If you're on Vraylar because an antidepressant alone wasn't enough, regular drinking can make it hard for you and your doctor to tell whether the treatment is working. Our guides to [antidepressants and alcohol](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol) and [alcohol and depression](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-depression) go into this in more detail.

**Anxiety and the morning after.** The jittery, dread-filled feeling the day after drinking (often called "hangxiety") is partly a rebound effect as alcohol wears off. If you're already prone to restlessness from akathisia, or to anxiety, that rebound can feel stronger. Our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) explains what's behind it.

**Schizophrenia.** Alcohol can worsen symptoms, make it harder to stick with treatment, and raise the risk of relapse. Added sedation and impaired judgment matter more when someone's thinking is already under strain.

### What about cariprazine for cutting down on drinking?

You may see cariprazine mentioned in research on addiction, because the D3 receptor it targets is involved in the brain's reward system. That research is early, and Vraylar isn't approved to treat alcohol use disorder. It doesn't mean drinking on Vraylar is safe, and it doesn't mean the medicine will reduce your cravings. If you'd like help cutting back, there are medicines approved for that purpose, and your doctor can walk you through them.

## Vraylar, Alcohol, and Sleep

Vraylar can cause **insomnia** in some people and **sleepiness** in others. Alcohol makes you drowsy at first, then breaks up sleep later in the night as it wears off. Put together, you can end up falling asleep heavily and then waking at 3 or 4 am, restless and unable to drift back off. If you notice this pattern, our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains the alcohol side of it. For the Vraylar side, ask your prescriber whether the time of day you take it could be adjusted; that's a decision to make with them, not on your own.

## Vraylar, Alcohol, and Blackouts

There's very little formal research on blackouts with cariprazine specifically. What's well established is that blackouts are mainly driven by how fast your blood alcohol rises, and that medicines which act on the brain can make a given amount of alcohol feel stronger. Many people on Vraylar also take other sedating medicines, which raises that risk further.

If you've had a blackout while on Vraylar, treat it as a sign the combination affects you more than you realize, and mention it to your prescriber. Our article on [blacking out from drinking](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) explains what's happening in the brain during one.

## Vraylar and Alcohol Side Effects to Watch For

These are the effects most likely to appear or get worse when you drink on Vraylar:

| Effect | Why it happens | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Unusual drowsiness or feeling "too drunk" | Both affect the brain and slow reactions | Stop drinking, stay with someone, don't drive |
| Dizziness or fainting when standing | Both can lower blood pressure; alcohol dehydrates | Sit or lie down, rise slowly, drink water |
| Unsteadiness and falls | Sedation plus low blood pressure | Avoid stairs and baths; have someone nearby |
| Restlessness that's worse the next day | Akathisia plus alcohol's sleep disruption | Tell your prescriber if it keeps happening |
| Waking in the early hours | Vraylar insomnia plus alcohol rebound | Track it; mention it at your next visit |
| Low mood or anxiety the day after | Alcohol rebound on top of a mood condition | Notice the pattern and bring it up with your prescriber |
| Overheating | Impaired temperature control plus dehydration | Get somewhere cool, drink water, seek help if confused |

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

Most people who have a drink on Vraylar will simply feel sleepier or dizzier than usual. But some signs mean you should get help now rather than waiting it out.

> **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if someone on Vraylar who has been drinking:**
>
> - Can't be woken up, or keeps drifting off and can't stay awake
> - Is breathing very slowly or irregularly, or making snoring or gurgling sounds while unresponsive
> - Vomits while very drowsy (roll them onto their side so they don't choke)
> - Faints, or falls and hits their head
> - Has a seizure
> - Develops a **high fever with stiff muscles, confusion, heavy sweating, or a racing heart**. This can be neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a rare but serious reaction to antipsychotics that needs emergency care.
>
> **If someone talks about suicide or hurting themselves, or you're worried they might, call or text 988** (US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline) or call 911. Stay with them if it's safe to do so. Outside the US, use your local emergency number.

For questions about a possible overdose or a mix of medicines and alcohol, **Poison Control is available at 1-800-222-1222** (US), any time. If you're not sure whether someone has had a dangerous amount to drink, our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) lists what to look for.

**Book a routine appointment with your prescriber if you notice:**

- Drinking has started to feel like the way you manage restlessness, sleep, or mood
- One or two drinks hit much harder than they used to
- Your mood swings more in weeks when you drink
- New movements you can't control, such as lip smacking, grimacing, or twitching (a possible sign of tardive dyskinesia, a known antipsychotic side effect)

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from combining Vraylar and alcohol if you:

- **Recently started Vraylar or changed your dose.** Because levels take weeks to settle, side effects can show up late.
- **Take other sedating medicines**, such as benzodiazepines like Xanax, sleep aids, gabapentin, opioids, or sedating antihistamines. Our [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) and [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) guides cover two common add-ons.
- **Take a medicine that blocks CYP3A4**, such as some antifungals or antibiotics. These raise cariprazine levels, and the label calls for a lower Vraylar dose. Higher levels mean more side effects for alcohol to stack on top of.
- **Have bipolar disorder**, where alcohol is a known trigger for mood episodes.
- **Are over 65**, when falls and low blood pressure are more dangerous.
- **Have diabetes or high triglycerides**, since both Vraylar and alcohol can affect them.
- **Have a seizure disorder or a history of heavy drinking.**
- **Drive for work** or operate machinery.

If any of these apply, have a frank conversation with your prescriber or pharmacist. If you've taken other medicines in this class, our guides to [Abilify and alcohol](/never-hungover/abilify-and-alcohol) [Seroquel and alcohol](/never-hungover/seroquel-and-alcohol), [olanzapine and alcohol](/never-hungover/olanzapine-and-alcohol), and [Latuda and alcohol](/never-hungover/latuda-and-alcohol) cover those, and our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) gives a wider overview.

## What About Hangover Supplements Like DHM?

If you're on Vraylar, the best hangover plan is the plainest one: drink little or nothing, eat first, drink water, and protect your sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence behind them.

Some readers ask about DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound sold as a hangover supplement. Here's the honest picture for someone on Vraylar:

- Most DHM research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. There is no good evidence that it reliably prevents hangovers in people.
- In animal studies, DHM acts on GABA-A receptors in the brain, part of the same system alcohol affects. That's why it's studied, but it also means it shouldn't be assumed to be neutral alongside other brain-active medicines.
- **There are no studies of DHM combined with cariprazine.** No one can tell you the combination is safe, because it hasn't been tested.
- DHM does **not** cancel out the drowsiness, dizziness, or judgment effects of mixing Vraylar and alcohol, and it won't make it safe to drive.

If you're curious about DHM, ask your prescriber or pharmacist first and bring the product label. We don't recommend hangover products on this page, because nothing you can buy makes drinking on Vraylar safer. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about DHM alongside common prescriptions. Don't start any supplement on your own while you're on an antipsychotic.

## The Bottom Line

- The safest choice is to **avoid alcohol** on Vraylar. The label warns about drowsiness, impaired judgment, dizziness, falls, and overheating, and alcohol makes each of those worse.
- The interaction isn't a chemical reaction in your blood. It's added impairment, plus alcohol working against the mood or thinking problems Vraylar treats.
- Cariprazine and its active metabolites last **weeks** in your body, so **timing your dose around a drink doesn't separate them**, and skipping doses won't help.
- If your prescriber is comfortable with an occasional drink, stick to the amount they set, with food and water, and don't drive afterward.
- Get emergency help for anyone who can't be woken, is breathing poorly, faints, has a seizure, or develops a high fever with stiff muscles. For thoughts of suicide, call or text 988.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Vraylar?**

The safest choice is to avoid it. Vraylar (cariprazine) and alcohol both act on the brain, and together they can increase drowsiness, dizziness, impaired judgment, and the risk of falls. The label warns about each of those. Some prescribers are comfortable with an occasional single drink for someone who has been stable on a low dose for a while, but that's a decision to make with your own prescriber, not a general rule.

**What happens if you drink on Vraylar?**

Most often you feel sleepier, dizzier, or more drunk than you'd expect from what you had, and you may feel light-headed when you stand up. Alcohol can also worsen Vraylar's restlessness (akathisia), break up your sleep, and make mood less stable over the next few days. Rarely, heavy drinking can lead to dangerous sedation, fainting, or falls. If someone can't be woken or is breathing poorly, call 911.

**How long after taking Vraylar can I drink alcohol?**

There's no safe gap within a day, or even a few days. Cariprazine has a half-life of about 2 to 4 days, and its main active metabolite lasts about 1 to 3 weeks. Once you're on regular dosing, the level of active drug in your blood is nearly constant around the clock, so taking your capsule in the morning and drinking at night doesn't separate them.

**Should I skip my Vraylar dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Because the active drug lasts weeks in your body, skipping a dose barely changes how much is in your system, so it doesn't make drinking safer. Missing doses can raise the chance of your symptoms coming back, and because cariprazine leaves so slowly, a relapse can creep up over weeks. Talk to your prescriber if you want more flexibility around alcohol.

**Is cariprazine and alcohol different from Vraylar and alcohol?**

No. Cariprazine is the active ingredient in Vraylar, so the alcohol advice is identical. Everything that applies to Vraylar applies to any cariprazine product.

**Does alcohol make Vraylar less effective?**

Alcohol isn't known to significantly change how your liver clears cariprazine, so it isn't expected to lower the drug level in your blood. But it works against the treatment in other ways: it disrupts sleep, can trigger mood episodes in bipolar disorder, deepens low mood in depression, and makes it harder for you and your doctor to judge whether Vraylar is working.

**Can Vraylar and alcohol cause blackouts?**

There's little research on blackouts with cariprazine specifically. Blackouts are mainly driven by how quickly blood alcohol rises, but brain-active medicines can make a given amount of alcohol hit harder, especially if you also take other sedating medicines. If you've blacked out on Vraylar, tell your prescriber, since it suggests the combination affects you more than you realize.

**Is it safe to take DHM while on Vraylar?**

There are no studies of DHM combined with cariprazine, so no one can say the combination is safe. DHM acts on brain GABA receptors in animal studies, so it isn't a neutral add-on to brain-active medicines, and it doesn't reduce the drowsiness or impairment from mixing Vraylar and alcohol. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist before trying it.
